parole.significato: a suffix forming masculine nouns, originally diminutives, occurring especially in words of Dutch and Flemish origin
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French -quin, -quain, from Middle Dutch -kin (compare Middle Low German -ken, German -chen), from Old Dutch *-kīn, from Proto-West Germanic *-ikīn, *-ukīn, a double diminutive formed from Proto-Germanic *-ukaz + Proto-Germanic *-īną. More at English -kin, -ock, -en.
Inherited from Old French escore, from Middle Dutch schore (“shore”).

Inherited from Middle French bague, possibly a borrowing from Middle Dutch bage, bagge (“ring”), of obscure origin, but likely from Old Frisian bāg, bāch (“ring”), from Proto-West Germanic *baug, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *baugaz (“ring, circlet”). Compare Middle Low German bâge, bôge (“curve,
Borrowed from Middle Dutch boechspriet (Modern Dutch boegspriet). Further reading below gives another etymology which might be more relevant as establishing word roots to older references.

Inherited from Middle French biere (early 15th c.), a borrowing from Middle Dutch bier and/or Middle High German bier, both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *beuzą. See beer for more. Displaced cervoise.
Borrowed from Middle Dutch blâsen (“to blow, sound, brag”), from Old Dutch *blāsan, from Proto-West Germanic *blāsan (“to blow”). Cognate with German blasen (“to blow”), Dutch blazen, English blast.

Past participle of blaser, from Middle Dutch blâsen (“to blow, sound, brag”), from Old Dutch *blāsan, from Proto-West Germanic *blāsan (“to blow”). Cognate with German blasen (“to blow”), English blast.

Inherited from Middle French bloc (“a considerable piece of something heavy, block”), from Old French bloc (“log, block”), from Middle Dutch blok (“treetrunk”), from Old Dutch *blok (“log”), from Frankish or Proto-West Germanic *blokk, from Proto-Germanic *blukką (“beam, log”).
Inherited from Middle French blocus, bloccus, from Middle Dutch blochuus.

parole.significato: to block (physically), to barricade, to obstruct
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French bloquer, from Middle Dutch blok, from Old Dutch *blok, from Proto-West Germanic *blokk, from Proto-Germanic *blukką.
Borrowed from Middle Dutch bote (“bundle of flax; tuft”), akin to Middle Low German bōte (“bundle of flax”).
Inherited from Old French bourgemaistre (with various variants), from Middle Dutch burchmeester and Middle High German burgemeister.

Partly from Middle Dutch boeye (“life buoy”); and partly continuing Middle French boue(e) (“a flotation signalling danger”), from Old French boue, buie (“a piece of wood or cork floating above an anchor to indicate where it is anchored”), ultimately from Frankish *baukn, from Proto-Germanic *baukną.

Most likely from Old French beguer, from Middle Dutch beggen (“to chat”) (related to beggaert (“one who rattles off prayers”)). This word itself is of uncertain origin, but could possibly be related to spreken (“to speak, tell”), lacking the initial s and r due to some substrate influence. Rejected

parole.significato: crush, fancy (a short-lived and unrequited love or infatuation)
parole.testo: Originally "child's bonnet," "nun's headdress," from Middle Dutch beggaert (“one who rattles off prayers”), which is from the same origin as Etymology 1 above. Compare embéguiner (“to be infatuated, have a crush on someone”).
Inherited from Middle French bellitre, belistre, belleudre, from Middle Dutch bedelster, bedelare (“beggar”), from bedelen (“to beg”), from Old Dutch *bedulon, from Proto-West Germanic *bedulōn.

Inherited from Middle French cabaret, from Middle Dutch cambret, from Old Northern French camberete and Picard Old French camberet (“little room”), diminutive of cambre (“chamber”) (modern chambre), all from Latin camera.
Inherited from Old French cabillau, from Middle Dutch cabeliau. Compare Modern Dutch kabeljauw, German Kabeljau.

Uncertain. The Trésor de la langue française suggests a derivation from Middle Dutch hotten (“to shake”) (see hocher). Other sources suggest a derivation from Latin quatiō, from Frankish *hottôn (see German hotzen), or that the word is onomatopoeic.
From Middle Dutch kabuys.

Inherited from Middle French claquer, from Old French claquer, clacquer (“to clack, clap, clatter”), from Middle Dutch klacken (“to clack, crack, whack, shake”), from Old Dutch *klakon, from Proto-Germanic *klakōną (“to clap, chirp”).
Inherited from Middle French clinc, from Middle Dutch klinken.

From Middle Dutch korf, korver (“a kind of ship”), or Middle Low German korf (“a kind of ship and basket”), + -ette. Possibly ultimately connected to Latin corbita (navis), "slow-sailing ship of burden, grain ship," which is from corbis.
From Middle French craquelin, from Old French craquelin, from Middle Dutch crakelinc (modern Dutch krakeling), from the verb craken (“to crack”).

Inherited from Middle French craquer, from Middle Dutch kraken (“to crack, crackle”), from Old Dutch *krakōn, from Frankish *krakōn (“to crack, crackle, shriek”), from Proto-Indo-European *gerg- (“to crow, shout”). Cognate with Old High German krahhōn, Old English cracian. More at crack.

parole.significato: fruit of any tree that is described under créquier
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French creke, creque, from Middle Dutch crieke, of unknown origin, see German Krieche for more.
From dandin + -er, or from Middle Dutch dantinnen (“to trifle”). More at dandle.

Inherited from Middle French digue, from Old French dike, diic, from Middle Dutch dijc (compare modern Dutch dijk), from Old Dutch diic, dīc, from Frankish *dīk, from Proto-Germanic *dīkaz (“pool”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to stick, stab, pierce, dig”). More at dig, dike, ditch.

parole.significato: to dam, to dike; to spur (a horse)
parole.testo: From Middle French diguer, dicquier, dieguer, from Old French dikier, from Middle Dutch diken, dijcken, from Old Dutch *dīkon, from Proto-West Germanic *dīkōn (“to dig, ditch, dam”); cognate with Old English dīcian (“to dam, dig”). More at English dig.
First attested in Middle French circa 1462, probably from Middle Dutch droge (modern Dutch droog).

Inherited from Middle French drolle (“a merry fellow, pleasant rascal”) from Old French drolle (“one who lives luxuriously”), from Middle Dutch drol (“fat little man, goblin”), itself from Old Norse troll, from Proto-Germanic *truzlą.

Inherited from Middle French dune, from Old French dune, from Middle Dutch dūne (modern Dutch duin), from Old Dutch dūn, dūno, from Proto-West Germanic *dūnā (“hill”), of uncertain origin. More at Proto-West Germanic *dūnā.

Inherited from Middle French desgringueler, from Old French gringoller, of Germanic origin, from Middle Dutch crinkelen, from kring (“circle”), from Old Dutch *kring, from Proto-Germanic *kringaz. The sense would refer to someone tumbling in successive circles.

parole.significato: a small piece of unburned coal mixed with ashes
parole.testo: Ultimately from Middle Dutch schrabben, schrabbelen (see modern Dutch schrapen (“scrape, rake”)).

From Middle French estoquer, from Old French estoquer, estochier ("to thrust, strike, stab"; compare Old French estoc (“a rapier”)), probably from Middle Dutch stoken (“to jab, thrust, poke”) or Middle High German stoken (“to jab, pierce”), both ultimately from Proto-Germanic *stukōną (“to be stiff,
From Old French flamenc, from Middle Dutch vlaminc.
Borrowed from Middle Dutch verlaten.

parole.significato: freight, cargo fees: the cost of transporting cargo by boat
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French fret, from Middle Dutch vrecht, from Old Dutch *frēht, from Proto-West Germanic *fra- + *aihti.
From Middle Dutch gredich.

From Middle French grommeler, from Old French grumeler (“to murmur, grumble”), from Middle Dutch grommelen (“to murmur, mutter, grunt”), frequentative of Middle Dutch grommen, related to Low German grummeln (“to grumble”), German grummeln (“to grumble”).

parole.significato: to mill about, swarm with people
parole.testo: From Middle French grouiller (“to shake, stir, agitate, scold, hasten, swarm, teem, crawl”), from Old French grouiller (“to rumble”), alteration of Old French grouller (“to growl”), from Middle Dutch grollen (“to make a noise, rumble, growl, grunt, grumble, scold”), from Old Dutch *grullen, from Pro
From Middle French gueux, probably from Middle Dutch guyte.

parole.significato: to ferment, to cause the yeast to overflow from the barrel/keg
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French ghiller, from Middle Dutch gilen (“to ferment”). The word was introduced into Walloon, Flemish and Picard at a time when the brewing industry was flourishing in the Low Country.

parole.significato: harbour (UK, Ireland, and the Commonwealth) / harbor (US)
parole.testo: Via Middle French, from Middle Dutch havene, from Old Dutch *havana, from Proto-West Germanic *habanu or more probably from Old Danish *hafn (Danish havn), from Old Norse hǫfn (“haven”), from Proto-Germanic *habnō. Cognate with English haven.

Inherited from Middle French houblon, houbelon (15th c.), from a confluence of two words: * Middle French hoppe, houppe (“hopped beer”, 14th c.), from Middle Dutch hoppe (“hops”), from Old Dutch *hoppo, from Frankish *hoppō (“hops”), of uncertain further origin. See English hop for more. * Old Frenc
Inherited from Middle French laie, from Middle Dutch lāde (“box”), from Old Dutch *latha, from Proto-Germanic *hlaþō. Compare Afrikaans laai.
From Middle French lambequin, perhaps from Middle Dutch lappekijn, lepperkijn, from Old Dutch lappakīn. By surface analysis, lambeau (“scrap, strip”) + -quin (diminutive suffix).
Inherited from Middle French leynge, lingue, from Middle Dutch *lenge.

parole.significato: a lip, especially the lower one when it is large or protruded
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French lippe, from Old French lipe, lepe (“underlip”), from Middle Dutch lippe (“lip”), from Frankish *lippjō (“lip”).

From Middle French loque, loc (“lock of hair; tuft of coarse wool”), from Middle Dutch locke (“curl”) or Middle English lok (“lock of hair”); both ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *lokk (“lock (of hair)”), from Proto-Germanic *lukkaz (“lock (of hair)”). More at English lock.
Borrowed from Middle Dutch manne, variant of mande.
Borrowed from Middle Dutch manneken, mannkijn.

Inherited from Middle French macquereau, maquereau, maqueriau, from Old French makerele, maquereau, from Middle Dutch makelaer, makelare (“broker”), itself from Old Frisian mek (“to marry”), from maken (“to make”), from Proto-West Germanic *makōn.
From Middle Dutch marcgrāve (modern Dutch markgraaf).

From Middle French matelot (“sailor”), from Old French matenot (“sailor, bunkmate”), most likely from Middle Dutch mattenoot (“bunk fellow”), corresponding to modern mat (“mat, rug, hammock”) + genoot (“companion”) or less likely Old Norse mǫtunautr (“food companion”) (from matr (“food”) + nautr (“c

Inherited from Middle French, from Old French mitte (“kind of insect which gnaws on cloth or cheese”), from Middle Dutch mīte (“moth, mite”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *mītǭ (“biting insect”, literally “cutter”), from *maitaną (“to cut”). Akin to Old English mīte (“mite, tiny insect”), Old High

From Middle French mocquer, from Old French moquer, from Middle Dutch mocken (“to mumble”) or Middle Low German mucken (“to grumble, speak with half-opened mouth”), both from Old Saxon *mokkian, *mukkian (“to low, mumble”), from Proto-Germanic *mukkijaną, *mūhaną (“to low, bellow, shout”), from Prot

parole.significato: a tuft of wool; a knot in a fabric; nap
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Dutch noppe (“a fluff of wool, wool tassel”), from Old Dutch *noppo, *hnoppo, from Proto-Germanic *hnuppô (“nap of cloth”), from Proto-Indo-European *knew-, *kenw- (“to scratch, scrape, rub”). Cognate with Old English hnoppa (“nap of cloth”). More at nap.
From Middle French paquet, from Middle Dutch pac (modern Dutch pak), from Old Dutch *pakko, from Frankish *pakkō, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô.
From Middle Dutch placken (“to patch, beat metal into a thin plate”), from placke (“disk, patch, stain”), from *Old Dutch plagga (“patch”), from Proto-Germanic *plaggą (“patch”).
From Middle French pompe, from Middle Dutch pompe (“device for raising water, pump”). Related to Middle Low German pumpe (“a pump”). More at pump.
A diminutive of Middle Dutch robbe (“rabbit”), of the family of German Robbe (“seal”) and English rabbit. Displaced in Old French plaine from Latin plāna (“plane”).

From Middle Dutch rammeken (“toasted bread”) or Middle Low German ramken (“cream”), from rame, rōme (“cream”), from Old Saxon *rōm (“cream”), from Proto-West Germanic *raum, from Proto-Germanic *raumaz (“cream”), from Proto-Indo-European *rewǝgh- (“to sour”). Cognate with Old High German roum (“crea

c. 1730, from re- + luquier, second part from Middle French luquier, from Old French luquier, borrowed from Middle Dutch loeken, from Old Dutch *lōkon, from Proto-West Germanic *lōkōn (“to look”), akin to English look.

parole.significato: furrow, channel (small trench cut in the soil or rock for irrigation or for planting seeds)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French regol, from Middle Dutch regel (“row”), from Latin rēgula (“straight line”). Doublet of rail, règle, reille, and rille.
From a form of Middle Dutch ringhband, from Proto-Germanic *hringaz + *bandą, *bandiz (“band, fetter”).
Borrowed from Middle Dutch stocvisch.
Inherited from Old French taquehan, from Middle Dutch takehan.

From Middle French trac, from Old French trac (“a track, trace, a beaten path, course”), from Middle Dutch treck, treke (“a drawing, draft, delineation, feature, train, procession, line or flourish with a pen, sketch”), from Old Dutch *trecken, from Proto-Germanic *trakjaną (“to drag”). More at trac
An alteration (with intrusive r) of Middle French tingle, from Middle Dutch tengel.
From Middle Dutch wacharme (“alas”).

From Middle French, from Middle Dutch wase (“mud, silt, wet ground, clod of dirt, grass”), from *Old Dutch waso, from Proto-Germanic *wasô (“moisture, ground”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“moist, wet”). More at ouze.
Inherited from Middle French wembelkin, from Middle Dutch wimmelkijn, diminutive of wimmel (“drill”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weyp- (“to turn”).

parole.significato: bulk (goods sold and transported unpackaged in large amounts)
parole.testo: From Middle French warac (“of lesser quality”, said of fish), from Middle Dutch wrac (“spoilt, defective”).
From Old French esbroer, probably a borrowing from Middle Dutch broeyen, from Proto-Germanic *brōaną (“to singe; to brew”).

From Middle French échoppe, from Old French eschope, escope, from Middle Dutch schoppe, scoppe, from Old Dutch *scoppa, from Proto-Germanic *skup- (“shed, stall”). Cognate with German Schupfen, Schuppen (“shed”), Dutch schop (“barn, shack”), English shop. More at shop.
Inherited from Middle French écran, from Old French escran, escren, borrowed from Middle Dutch scherm, from Old Dutch *skirm, from Proto-West Germanic *skirmi, from Proto-Germanic *skirmiz.

Alteration of Middle French esclefin (probably after aigle), originally borrowed from Middle Dutch schelvisch, modern Dutch schelvis, corresponding to schel (“skin, rind”) (modern Dutch schil) + vis (“fish”).
From Middle Dutch spierlinc.

Inherited from Middle French estriquer, borrowed from Middle Dutch striken (“to stroke, smooth”), from Old Dutch *strīcan. Cognate with English strike. Compare also Old French estrikier, estriquer (“to strike”).

Inherited from Middle French amarer (14th c.), from Middle Dutch *aenmâren, from aen (“on”) + mâren (“to moor, dock, fasten a ship”), a variant of mêren, from Proto-West Germanic *mairōn, whence English moor. Inherited from Middle French boucquain (“old book of little esteem”), from a derivative of Middle Dutch boec (“book”). Either from an unrecorded Middle Dutch *boekijn, a possible variant of the usual interfixed diminutives boecskin, boekelkin; or instead a native French derivation from the Middle Du
Uncertain. Probably from Italian facchino or, alternatively, from Middle French facque (from Middle Dutch fac (“compartment, closed space”), corresponding to modern Dutch vak) + -in.
